title: Risk Phase Transitions in Spiked Regression: Alignment Driven Benign and Catastrophic Overfitting
claim: Whether alignment with a dominant direction helps or hurts generalization depends on how its strength scales, producing benign, tempered or catastrophic overfitting.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared axes, caption text under each panel
description: Two side-by-side line plots with a gray grid background. Each plots excess error (y-axis) against the overparameterization ratio c = d/n (x-axis). Each plot has two series: aligned targets (red circles, solid line) and anti-aligned targets (blue squares, dashed line). In both panels the error rises to a sharp double-descent peak of about 20 near c = 1, then falls. In the left panel (operator-norm scaling), the aligned curve dips, then climbs linearly to about 22 at c = 10, while the anti-aligned curve levels off near 8. In the right panel (equal-Frobenius scaling), the aligned curve decays toward 0 while the anti-aligned curve plateaus near 7. Captions below name the regime in each panel. The eye goes first to the tall peak, then to the diverging red and blue curves.
caption: Excess error vs. overparameterization ratio c = d/n in the well-specified case. Each plot shows the risk for aligned and anti-aligned targets under different spike scaling regimes. The scatter plots are empirically obtained and the lines are theory.
abstract: This paper analyzes the generalization error of minimum-norm interpolating solutions in linear regression using spiked covariance data models. The paper characterizes how varying spike strengths and target-spike alignments can affect risk, especially in overparameterized settings. The study presents an exact expression for the generalization error, leading to a comprehensive classification of benign, tempered, and catastrophic overfitting regimes based on spike strength, the aspect ratio $c=d/n$ (particularly as $c \to \infty$), and target alignment. Notably, in well-specified aligned problems, increasing spike strength can surprisingly induce catastrophic overfitting before achieving benign overfitting. The paper also reveals that target-spike alignment is not always advantageous, identifying specific, sometimes counterintuitive, conditions for its benefit or detriment. Alignment with the spike being detrimental is empirically demonstrated to persist in nonlinear models.
